Thus Paul had begun the good work at Ephesus, thus free had he been of his pains; and why then should they be sparing of their pains in carrying it on? <div eID="gen29996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29997" type="x-p"/> V. He recommends them to divine direction and influence (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.32">v. 32</reference>): "<hi type="italic">And now, brethren,</hi> having given you this solemn charge and caution, <hi type="italic">I commend you to God.</hi> Now that I have said what I have to say, The Lord be with you; I must leave you, but I leave you in good hands." They were in care what would become of them, how they should go on in their work, break through their difficulties, and what provision would be made for them and their families. In answer to all these perplexities, Paul directs them to look up to God with an eye of faith, and beseeches God to look down on them with an eye of favour. <div eID="gen29997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29998" type="x-p"/> 1. See here to whom he commends them. He calls them brethren, not only as Christians, but as ministers, and thereby encourages them to hope in God, as he had done; for they and he were brethren. (1.) He commends them to God, begs of God to provide for them, to take care of them, and to supply all their needs, and encourages them to cast all their care upon him, with an assurance that he cared for them: "Whatever you want, go to God, let your eye be ever towards him, and your dependence upon him, in all your straits and difficulties; and let this be your comfort, that you have a God to go to, a God all sufficient." <hi type="italic">I commend you to God,</hi> that is, to his providence, and to the protection and care of that. It is enough that, from whomsoever we are separated, still we have God nigh unto us, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.19">1 Pet. iv. 19</reference>. (2.) He commends them <hi type="italic">to the word of his grace,</hi> by which some understand Christ: he is <hi type="italic">the word</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.1">John i. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">the word of life,</hi> because life is treasured up for us in him (<reference osisRef="1John.1.1">1 John i. 1</reference>), and in the same sense he is here called <hi type="italic">the word of God's grace,</hi> because <hi type="italic">from his fulness we receive grace for grace.</hi> He commends them to Christ, puts them into his hand, as being his servants, whom he would in a particular manner take care of. Paul commends them not only to God and to his providence, but to Christ and his grace as Christ himself did his disciples when he was leaving them: <hi type="italic">You believe in God, believe also in me.</hi> It comes to much the same thing, if by the word of his grace we understand the gospel of Christ, for it is Christ in the word that is nigh unto us for our support and encouragement, and his word is spirit and life: "You will find much relief by acting faith on the providence of God, but much more by acting faith on the promises of the gospel." He commends them to the word of Christ's grace, which he spoke to his disciples when he sent them forth, the commission he gave them, with assurance that he would be with them <hi type="italic">always to the end of the world:</hi> "Take hold of that word, and God give you the benefit and comfort of it, and you need no more." He commends them to the word of God's grace, not only as the foundation of their hope and the fountain of their joy, but as the rule of their walking: "<hi type="italic">I commend you to God,</hi> as your Master, whom you are to serve, and I have found him a good Master, <hi type="italic">and to the word of his grace,</hi> as cutting you out your work, and by which you are to govern yourselves; observe the precepts of this word, and then live upon the promises of it." <div eID="gen29998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29999" type="x-p"/> 2. See here what he commends them to the word of God's grace for, not so much for a protection from their enemies, or a provision for their families, as for the spiritual blessings which they most needed and ought most to value. They had received the gospel of the grace of God, and were entrusted to preach it. Now he recommends them to that, (1.) For their edification: "<hi type="italic">It is able</hi> (the Spirit of grace working with it and by it) <hi type="italic">to build you up,</hi> and you may depend upon this, while you keep close to it, and are deriving daily from it. Though you are already furnished with good gifts, yet this is able to build you up; there is that in it with which you need to be better acquainted and more affected." Note, Ministers, in preaching the word of grace, must aim at their own edification as well as at the edification of others. The most advanced Christians, while they are in this world, are capable of growing, and they will find the word of grace to have still more and more in it to contribute to their growth. It is still able to build them up. (2.) For their glorification: <hi type="italic">It is able to give you an inheritance among all those who are sanctified.</hi> The word of God's grace gives it, not only as it gives the knowledge of it (for <hi type="italic">life and immortality are brought to light by the gospel</hi>), but as it gives the promise of it, the promise of a God <hi type="italic">that cannot lie,</hi> and which is <hi type="italic">yea and amen in Christ;</hi> and by the word, as the ordinary vehicle, the Spirit of grace is given (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.44">ch. x. 44</reference>), to be the seal of the promise, and the earnest of the eternal life promised; and thus it is the word of God's grace that gives us the inheritance. Note, [1.] Heaven is an inheritance which gives an indefeasible right to all the heirs; it is an inheritance like that of the Israelites in Canaan, which was by promise and yet by lot, but was <hi type="italic">sure to all the seed.</hi> [2.] This inheritance is entailed upon and secured to all those, and those only, that are sanctified; for as those cannot be welcome guests to the holy God, or the holy society above, that are unsanctified, so really heaven would be no heaven to them; but <hi type="italic">to all that are sanctified,</hi> that are born again, and on whom the image of God is renewed, it is as sure as almighty power and eternal truth can make it. Those therefore that would make out a title to that inheritance must make it sure that they are among the sanctified, are joined to them and incorporated with them, and partake of the same image and nature; for we cannot expect to be among the glorified hereafter unless we be among the sanctified here. <div eID="gen29999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30000" type="x-p"/> VI. He recommends himself to them as an example of indifference to this world, and to every thing in it, which, if they would walk in the same spirit and in the same steps, they would find to contribute greatly to their easy and comfortable passage through it. He had recommended them to God, and to the word of his grace, for spiritual blessings, which, without doubt, are the best blessings; but what shall they do for food for their families, an agreeable subsistence for themselves, and portions for their children? "As to these," Paul says, "do as I did;" and how was that? He here tells them, <div eID="gen30000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30001" type="x-p"/> 1. That he never aimed at worldly wealth (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.33">v. 33</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I have coveted no man's silver, or gold, or apparel;</hi> nor do you, and then you will be easy." There were many in Ephesus, and many of those that had embraced the Christian faith, who were rich, had a great deal of money, and plate, and rich furniture, and wore very good clothes, and made a very good appearance. Now, (1.) Paul was not ambitious to live like them. We may take it in this sense: "<hi type="italic">I never coveted to have so much silver and gold at command</hi> as I see others have, nor to wear such rich clothes as I see others wear. I neither condemn them nor envy them. I can live comfortably and usefully without living great." The false apostles desired <hi type="italic">to make a fair show in the flesh</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.12">Gal. vi. 12</reference>), to make a figure in the world; but Paul did not do so. <hi type="italic">He knew how to want and how to be abased.</hi> (2.) He was not greedy to receive from them, silver, or gold, or apparel; so far from being always craving that he was not so much as coveting, nor desired them to allow him so and so for his pains among them, but was <hi type="italic">content with such things as he had;</hi> he never <hi type="italic">made a gain of them,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.17">2 Cor. xii. 17</reference>. He could not only say with Moses (<reference osisRef="Num.16.15">Num. xvi. 15</reference>), and with Samuel (<reference osisRef="1Sam.12.3">1 Sam. xii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.5">5</reference>), <hi type="italic">Whose ox have I taken? Or whom have I defrauded?</hi> But, "Whose kindness have I coveted, or asked? Or to whom have I been burdensome?" He protests against desiring a gift, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.17">Phil. iv. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen30001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30002" type="x-p"/> 2. That he had worked for his living, and taken a great deal of pains to get bread (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.34">v. 34</reference>) "<hi type="italic">Yea, you yourselves know,</hi> and have been eye-witnesses of it, <hi type="italic">that these hands of mine have ministered to my necessities, and to those that were with me;</hi> you have seen me busy early and late, cutting out tents and making them up;" and, they being commonly made of leather, it was very hard work. Observe, (1.) Paul was sometimes reduced to necessities, and the want of the common supports of life, though he was so great a favourite of Heaven and so great a blessing to this earth. What an unthinking, unkind, and ungrateful world is this, that could let such a man as Paul be poor in it! (2.) He desired no more than to have his necessities supplied; he did not work at his calling to enrich himself, but to maintain himself with food and raiment. (3.) When he was to earn his bread, he did it by a manual occupation. Paul had a head and a tongue that he might have got money by, but they were these hands, saith he, <hi type="italic">that ministered to my necessities.</hi> What a pity was it that those hands by the laying on of which the Holy Ghost had been so often conferred, those hands by which God had wrought special miracles, and both these at Ephesus too (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.6">ch. xix. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.19.11">11</reference>), should there be obliged to lay themselves to the needle and shears, the awl and tacking-end, in tent-making, purely to get bread! Paul puts these presbyters (and others in them) in mind of this, that they may not think it strange if they be thus neglected, and yet to go on in their work, and make the best shift they can to live; the less encouragement they have from men, the more they shall have from God. (4.) He worked not only for himself, but for the support of those also that were with him. This was hard indeed. It had better become them to have worked for him (to maintain him as their tutor) than he for them. But so it is; those that are willing to take the labouring oar will find those about them willing they should have it. If Paul will work for the maintenance of his companions, he is welcome to do it.
entries.50ff7359b386b38ba453ef9013ebd83c0752fc4e: <div eID="gen30002" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Paul Takes Leave of the Elders of Ephesus.</title> <div sID="gen30003" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">36</hi> And when he had thus spoken, he kneeled down, and prayed with them all. <hi type="super">37</hi> And they all wept sore, and fell on Paul's neck, and kissed him, <hi type="super">38</hi> Sorrowing most of all for the words which he spake, that they should see his face no more. And they accompanied him unto the ship. <div eID="gen30003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30004" type="x-p"/> After the parting sermon that Paul preached to the elders of Ephesus, which was very affecting, we have here the parting prayer and tears, which were yet more affecting; we can scarcely read the account here given of them, and meditate upon them with dry eyes. <div eID="gen30004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30005" type="x-p"/> I. They parted with prayer (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.36">v. 36</reference>): <hi type="italic">And, when he had thus spoken, he kneeled down, and prayed with them all.</hi> And, no doubt, it was a prayer every way suited to the present mournful occasion. He committed them to God in this prayer, prayed that he would not leave them, but continue his presence with them. 1. It was a joint prayer. He not only prayed for them, but prayed with them, <hi type="italic">prayed with them all;</hi> that they might put up the same petitions for themselves and one another that he put up to God for them all, and that they might learn what to ask of God for themselves when he was gone. Public prayers are so far from being intended to supersede our own secret prayers, and make them needless, that they are designed to quicken and encourage them, and to direct us in them. When we are alone we should pray over the prayers that our ministers have put up with us. 2. It was a humble reverent prayer. This was expressed by the posture they used: <hi type="italic">He kneeled down, and prayed with them,</hi> which is the most proper gesture in prayer, and significant both of adoration and of petition, especially petition for the forgiveness of sin. Paul used it much: <hi type="italic">I bow my knees,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.14">Eph. iii. 14</reference>. 3. It was a prayer after sermon; and, we may suppose, he prayed over what he had preached. He had committed the care of the church at Ephesus to those elders, and now he prays that God would enable them faithfully to discharge this great trust reposed in them, and would give them those measures of wisdom and grace which it required; he prayed for the flock, and all that belonged to it, <hi type="italic">that the great Shepherd of the sheep</hi> would take care of them all, and keep them from being a prey to the grievous wolves. Thus he taught these ministers to pray for those they preached to, <hi type="italic">that they might not labour in vain.</hi> 4. It was a parting prayer, which might be likely to leave lasting impressions, as the farewell sermon did. It is good for friends, when they part, to part with prayer, that by praying together just at parting they may be enabled to pray the more feelingly one for another when they are separated, which is one part of our Christian duty, and an improvement of the communion of saints. The Lord watch between us, and watch over us both, when we are absent one from the other, is a good parting prayer (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.49">Gen. xxxi. 49</reference>), as also that our next meeting may be either nearer heaven or in heaven. Paul here followed the example of Christ, who, when he took leave of his disciples, after he had preached to them, prayed with them all, <reference osisRef="John.17.1">John xvii. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen30005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30006" type="x-p"/> II. They parted with tears, abundance of tears, and most affectionate embraces, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.37-Acts.20.38">v. 37, 38</reference>. 1. <hi type="italic">They all wept sorely.</hi> We have reason to think the Paul himself began; though he was determined to go, and saw his call clear to other work, yet he was sorry in his heart to leave them, and many a tear it cost him. He that was so often in tears while he was with them (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.19">v. 19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.31">31</reference>), no doubt shed many at parting, so watering what he had sown among them. But the notice is taken of their tears: <hi type="italic">They all wept sorely;</hi> there was not a dry eye among them, and it is probable the affectionate expressions Paul used in prayer set them a-weeping. These were tears of love and mutual endearment, like those of Jonathan and David, when they were forced to part, and <hi type="italic">wept one with another, until</hi> (as if they wept for strife) <hi type="italic">David exceeded,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.41">1 Sam. xx. 41</reference>. 2. <hi type="italic">They fell upon Paul's neck, and kissed him,</hi> all, one after another, each bewailing his own loss: "How can I part with this invaluable man, this blessed Paul," says one, "in whom my life is a manner bound up?"—"Farewell, my dear friend," says another, "a thousand thanks to thee, and ten thousand to God for thee, and for all the pains thou hast taken with me for my good." "And must we part?" says another: "must I lose my spiritual father, nurse, and guide?"—"What will become of us now?" says another, "when we shall no more have him to apply to, and receive direction from? What shall I do, if the Lord take away my master from my head? <hi type="italic">My father, my father, the chariots of Israel, and the horsemen thereof.</hi>" Note, Those that are most loving are commonly best beloved. Paul, who was a most affectionate friend himself, had friends that were very affectionate to him. These tears at parting with Paul were a grateful return for all the tears he had shed in preaching to them and praying with them. <hi type="italic">He that watereth shall be watered also himself.</hi> 3. That which cut them to the heart thus, and made this place such a <hi type="italic">Bochim, such a place of weepers,</hi> was, <hi type="italic">that word which Paul spoke, that</hi> he was certain <hi type="italic">they should see his face no more.</hi> If he had given them directions to follow him, as he did to those that were his usual companions, or any intimation that he would come hereafter and make them a visit, they could have borne this parting pretty well; but when they are told that they shall see his face no more in this world, that it is a final farewell they are now giving and taking, this makes it a great mourning; it makes farewell just like a funeral, and puts them into this passion of weeping. There were other things for which they sorrowed—that they should lose the benefit of his public performances, and see him no longer presiding in their assemblies, should have none of his personal counsels and comforts; and, we hope, they sorrowed for their own sin, in not profiting more by his labours while they had him among them, and which had provoked God to order his remove. But that which gave the most sensible accent to their grief was <hi type="italic">that they should see his face no more.</hi> When our friends are separated from us by death, this is the consideration with which we raise up our mourning, that we shall see their faces no more; but we complain of this as those that have no hope, for if our friends died in Christ, and we live to him, they are gone to see God's face, to behold his glory, with the reflection of which their faces shine, and we hope to be with them shortly. Though we shall see their faces no more in this world, we hope to see them again in a better world, and to be there together for ever and with the Lord. <div eID="gen30006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30007" type="x-p"/> III. They <hi type="italic">accompanied him unto the ship,</hi> partly to show their respect for him (they would bring him on his way as far as they could), and partly that they might have a little more of his company and conversation; if it must be the last interview, they will have as much of him as they can, and see the last of him. And we have reason to think that when they came to the water-side, and he was about to go on board, their tears and embraces were repeated; for loth to part bids oft farewell. But this was a comfort to both sides, and soon turned this tide of passion, that the presence of Christ both went with him and staid with them.  <chapter eID="Acts.20"/> <div eID="gen30007" type="x-p"/>

entries.021f2944b74c605d871737d06b641f07398ef632: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16092"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 20</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Acts.20.1-Acts.20.12">Ac 20:1-12</reference>. Paul Fulfils His Purpose of Proceeding Again to Macedonia and Greece--Returning Thence, on His Route for Jerusalem, He Revisits Philippi and Troas--His Ministrations at Troas.</title> <div sID="gen31102" type="x-p"/> This section of the apostle's life, though peculiarly rich in material, is related with great brevity in the History. Its details must be culled from his own Epistles.<div eID="gen31102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31103" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16092"/><hi type="bold">1-2. departed--</hi>after Pentecost (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.8">1Co 16:8</reference>).<div eID="gen31103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31104" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to go into Macedonia--</hi>in pursuance of the first part of his plan (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.21">Ac 19:21</reference>). From his Epistles we learn; (1) That, as might have been expected from its position on the coast, he revisited Troas (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">2Co 2:12</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Acts.16.8">Ac 16:8</reference>). (2) That while on his former visit he appears to have done no missionary work there, he now went expressly "to preach Christ's Gospel," and found "a door opened unto him of the Lord" there, which he entered so effectually as to lay the foundation of a church there (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.6">Ac 20:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.7">7</reference>). (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.3">3</reference>) That he would have remained longer there but for his uneasiness at the non-arrival of Titus, whom he had despatched to Corinth to finish the collection for the poor saints at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.1">1Co 16:1</reference>, 2; <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.6">2Co 8:6</reference>), but still more, that he might bring him word what effect his first Epistle to that church had produced. (He had probably arranged that they should meet at Troas). (4) That in this state of mind, afraid of something wrong, he "took leave" of the brethren at Troas, and went from thence into Macedonia.<div eID="gen31104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31105" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">It was, no doubt, the city of Philippi that he came to (landing at Nicopolis, its seaport, see on <reference osisRef="Acts.16.11">Ac 16:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.12">12</reference>), as appears by comparing <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.9">2Co 11:9</reference>, where "Macedonia" is named, with <reference osisRef="Phil.4.15">Php 4:15</reference>, where it appears that Philippi is meant. Here he found the brethren, whom he had left on his former visit in circumstances of such deep interest, a consolidated and thriving church, generous and warmly attached to their father in Christ; under the superintendence, probably, of our historian, "the beloved physician" (see on <reference osisRef="Acts.16.40">Ac 16:40</reference>). All that is said by our historian of this Macedonian visit is that "he went over those parts and gave them much exhortation." (5) Titus not having reached Philippi as soon as the apostle, "his flesh had no rest, but he was troubled on every side: without were fightings, within were fears" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.7.5">2Co 7:5</reference>). (<reference osisRef="2Cor.7.6">6</reference>) At length Titus arrived, to the joy of the apostle, the bearer of better tidings from Corinth than he had dared to expect (<reference osisRef="2Cor.7.6">2Co 7:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.13">7, 13</reference>), but checkered by painful intelligence of the efforts of a hostile party to undermine his apostolic reputation there (2Co 10:1-18). (7) Under the mixed feelings which this produced, he wrote--</hi>from Macedonia, and probably Philippi--his Second Epistle to the Corinthians (see Introduction to Second Corinthians); despatching Titus with it, and along with him two other unnamed deputies, expressly chosen to take up and bring their collection for the poor saints at Jerusalem, and to whom he bears the beautiful testimony, that they were "the glory of Christ" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.22">2Co 8:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.23">23</reference>). (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.8">8</reference>) It must have been at this time that he penetrated as far as to the confines of "Illyricum," lying along the shores of the Adriatic (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.19">Ro 15:19</reference>). He would naturally wish that his second Letter to the Corinthians should have some time to produce its proper effect ere he revisited them, and this would appear a convenient opportunity for a northwestern circuit, which would enable him to pay a passing visit to the churches at Thessalonica and Berea, though of this we have no record. On his way southward to Greece, he would preach the Gospel in the intermediate regions of Epirus, Thessaly, and Boeotia (see <reference osisRef="Rom.15.19">Ro 15:19</reference>), though of this we have no record. <div eID="gen31105" type="x-p"/>
entries.4ca4ddbe2acfdd10410603467e8c49d9801720ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16094"/><div sID="gen31107" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16094"/><hi type="bold">3. And there abode three months--</hi>Though the province only is here mentioned, it is the city of Corinth that is meant, as the province of "Macedonia" (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.1">Ac 20:1</reference>) meant the city of Philippi. Some rough work he anticipated on his arrival at Corinth (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.1-2Cor.8.11">2Co 10:1-8, 11</reference>; 13:1-10) though he had reason to expect satisfaction on the whole; and as we know there were other churches in Achaia besides that at Corinth (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.1">2Co 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.10">11:10</reference>), he would have time enough to pay them all a brief visit during the three months of his stay there. This period was rendered further memorable by the despatch of the Epistle to the Romans, written during his stay at Corinth and sent by "Phoebe, a servant [deaconess] of the Church at Cenchrea" (see on <reference osisRef="Acts.18.3">Ac 18:3</reference>), a lady apparently of some standing and substance, who was going thither on private business. (See on <reference osisRef="Rom.16.1">Ro 16:1</reference> and see Introduction to Romans).<div eID="gen31107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31108" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And when the Jews laid wait for him, as he was about to sail into Syria--</hi>He had intended to embark, probably at Cenchrea, the eastern harbor of the city, for Palestine, on his route to Jerusalem, the third part of his plan (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.21">Ac 19:21</reference>). But having detected some conspiracy against his life by his bitter Jewish enemies as at Damascus (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.22-Acts.9.25">Ac 9:22-25</reference>) and Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.29">Ac 9:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.30">30</reference>), he changed his plan and determined "to return" as he had come, "through Macedonia." As he was never more to return to Corinth, so this route would bring him, for the last time, face to face with the attached disciples of Berea, Thessalonica, and Philippi. <div eID="gen31108" type="x-p"/>
entries.651b8b0ea2beba36bbcb99291fab95c0fd68bd81: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16095"/><div sID="gen31109" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16095"/><hi type="bold">4-5. there accompanied him into Asia--</hi>the province of Asia.<div eID="gen31109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31110" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Sopater of Berea--</hi>The true reading, beyond doubt, is, "Sopater [the son] of Pyrrhus of Berea." Some think this mention of his father was to distinguish him from Sosipater (the same name in fuller form), mentioned in <reference osisRef="Rom.16.21">Ro 16:21</reference>. But that they were the same person seems more probable.<div eID="gen31110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31111" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Acts.19.29">Ac 19:29</reference>).<div eID="gen31111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31112" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and Secundus--</hi>of whom nothing else is known.<div eID="gen31112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31113" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Gaius of Derbe--</hi>Though the Gaius of <reference osisRef="Acts.19.29">Ac 19:29</reference> is said to be of "Macedonia," and this one "of Derbe," there is no sufficient reason for supposing them different persons; on the contrary, <reference osisRef="Rom.16.23">Ro 16:23</reference> (compare with 3Jo 1, where there is hardly any reason to doubt that the same Gaius is addressed) seems to show that though he spent an important part of his Christian life away from his native Derbe, he had latterly retired to some place not very far from it.<div eID="gen31113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31114" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and Timotheus--</hi>not probably of Derbe, as one might suppose from this verse, but of Lystra (see on <reference osisRef="Acts.16.1">Ac 16:1</reference>); both being so associated in his early connection with the apostle that the mention of the one in the previous clause would recall the other on the mention of his name.<div eID="gen31114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31115" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and of Asia, Tychicus and Trophimus--</hi>The latter was an Ephesian, and probably the former also. They seem to have put themselves, from this time forward, at the apostle's disposal, and to the very last been a great comfort to him (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.21">Ep 6:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.22">22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.4.7">Col 4:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.4.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.21.29">Ac 21:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.12">2Ti 4:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.20">20</reference>). From the mention of the places to which each of these companions belonged, and still more the order in which they occur, we are left to conclude that they were deputies from their respective churches, charged with taking up and bringing on the collection for the poor saints at Jerusalem, first at Berea, next at Thessalonica, then at Philippi [Howson], where we gather that our historian himself rejoined the party (from the resumption at <reference osisRef="Acts.20.5">Ac 20:5</reference> of the "us," dropped at <reference osisRef="Acts.16.17">Ac 16:17</reference>), by whom the Philippian collection would naturally be brought on. <div eID="gen31115" type="x-p"/>
entries.275d97d386e1a960c4edbc840ba652f339dacfba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16098"/><div sID="gen31122" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16098"/><hi type="bold">7. upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together--</hi>This, compared with <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.2">1Co 16:2</reference>, and other similar allusions, plainly indicates that the Christian observance of the day afterwards distinctly called "the Lord's Day," was already a fixed practice of the churches.<div eID="gen31122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31123" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Paul preached--</hi>discoursed. The tense implies continued action--"kept discoursing." <div eID="gen31123" type="x-p"/>
entries.20beba0e340373284cf0cfa7127cb91cdaf4710e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16099"/><div sID="gen31124" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16099"/><hi type="bold">8. there were many lights in the upper chamber--</hi>not a mere piece of graphic detail by an eye-witness [Hackett, Howson], but mentioned, probably, as increasing the heat and contributing to drowsiness [Webster and Wilkinson], as the next clause seems to show. <div eID="gen31124" type="x-p"/>
entries.5a1e6736d49acd6457cb5b6cf8a9b558144f04a0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16100"/><div sID="gen31125" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16100"/><hi type="bold">9. in a--</hi>"the."<div eID="gen31125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31126" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">window--</hi>or window seat, or recess.<div eID="gen31126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31127" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fell down from the third loft--</hi>"story."<div eID="gen31127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31128" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and was taken up dead--</hi>"The window projected (according to the side of the room where it was situated) either over the street or over the interior court; so that in either case he fell on the hard earth or pavement below." <div eID="gen31128" type="x-p"/>
entries.cb60ee41e4c6d40f7cc99ab509610ad1a02f5e82: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16101"/><div sID="gen31129" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16101"/><hi type="bold">10-12. Paul ... fell on him--</hi>like Elisha (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.34">2Ki 4:34</reference>).<div eID="gen31129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31130" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his life is in him--</hi>now restored; compare <reference osisRef="Mark.5.39">Mr 5:39</reference>. <div eID="gen31130" type="x-p"/>
entries.e644fdac7e54589c48dc66730de25e931025d3b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16103"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Acts.20.13-Acts.20.38">Ac 20:13-38</reference>. Continuing His Route to Jerusalem He Reaches Miletus, Whence He Sends for the Elders of Ephesus--His Farewell Address to Them.</title> <div sID="gen31133" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16103"/><hi type="bold">13-14. we ... sailed--</hi>from Troas.<div eID="gen31133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31134" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto Assos; there ... to take in Paul: for so had he appointed, minding himself to go afoot--</hi>"to go by land." (See on <reference osisRef="Mark.6.33">Mr 6:33</reference>). In sailing southward from Troas to Assos, one has to round Cape Lecture, and keeping due east to run along the northern shore of the Gulf of Adramyttium, on which it lies. This is a sail of nearly forty miles; whereas by land, cutting right across, in a southeasterly direction, from sea to sea, by that excellent Roman road which then existed, the distance was scarcely more than half. The one way Paul wished his companions to take, while he himself, longing perhaps to enjoy a period of solitude, took the other, joining the ship, by appointment, at Assos. <div eID="gen31134" type="x-p"/>
entries.e7d512339ecdf0b84263f882fcc1d90d339d6c44: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16105"/><div sID="gen31136" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16105"/><hi type="bold">15-16. came the next day over against Chios--</hi>now Scio: one of the most beautiful of those islands between which and the coast the sail is so charming. They appear not to have touched at it.<div eID="gen31136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31137" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">next day we arrived--</hi>"touched" or "put in."<div eID="gen31137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31138" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at Samos--</hi>another island coming quite close to the mainland, and about as far south of Chios as it is south of Lesbos.<div eID="gen31138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31139" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tarried--</hi>for the night.<div eID="gen31139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31140" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at Trogyllium--</hi>an anchorage on the projecting mainland, not more than a mile from the southern extremity of the island of Samos.<div eID="gen31140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31141" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">next day we came to Miletus--</hi>on the mainland; the ancient capital of Ionia, near the mouth of the Meander. <div eID="gen31141" type="x-p"/>
entries.66b741e8be9d918eda49b644543f7f94585a1e55: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16107"/><div sID="gen31146" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16107"/><hi type="bold">17. from Miletus he sent to Ephesus, and called the elders of the church--</hi>As he was now some forty miles south of Ephesus, we might think that more time would be lost by sending thus far for the elders to come to him, than by going at once to Ephesus itself, when so near it. But if unfavorable winds and stormy weather had overtaken them, his object could not have been attained, and perhaps he was unwilling to run the risk of detention at Ephesus by the state of the church and other causes. Those here called "elders" or "presbyters," are in <reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">Ac 20:28</reference> called "bishops." (See on <reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">Ac 20:28</reference>). The identity of presbyters and bishops in the New Testament is beyond all reasonable dispute. <div eID="gen31146" type="x-p"/>
entries.05e4d925a0c36aea1b28262a9d75bc3ba7ab80e3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16108"/><div sID="gen31147" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16108"/><hi type="bold">18. Ye know ... after what manner I have been with you at all seasons--</hi>For the Christian integrity and fidelity of his whole official intercourse with them he appeals to themselves. <div eID="gen31147" type="x-p"/>
entries.4cd7627bb83030dbb5ffb5536009f08aa164f089: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16109"/><div sID="gen31148" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16109"/><hi type="bold">19. Serving the Lord--</hi>Jesus.<div eID="gen31148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31149" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with all humility ... and many tears and temptations--</hi>Self-exaltation was unknown to him, and ease of mind: He "sowed in tears," from anxieties both on account of the converts from whom he "travailed in birth," and of the Jews, whose bitter hostility was perpetually plotting against him, interrupting his work and endangering his life. <div eID="gen31149" type="x-p"/>
entries.14f69920cd41cc6f20e706a50d3cc07f40c415ce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16110"/><div sID="gen31150" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16110"/><hi type="bold">20. kept back--</hi>timidly withheld from fear of consequences.<div eID="gen31150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31151" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nothing that was profitable--</hi>edification directing all.<div eID="gen31151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31152" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have taught you publicly, and from house to house--</hi>Did an apostle, whose functions were of so wide a range, not feel satisfied without private as well as public ministrations? How then must pastors feel? [Bengel]. <div eID="gen31152" type="x-p"/>
entries.673033a346c72c17c6e475cc3d8dec465f85ca15: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16111"/><div sID="gen31153" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16111"/><hi type="bold">21. Testifying both to Jews and ... Greeks--</hi>laboring under a common malady, and recoverable only by a common treatment.<div eID="gen31153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31154" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Acts.5.31">Ac 5:31</reference>). Repentance, as distinguished from faith, is that state of the "honest and good heart" which arises from a discovery of one's contrariety to the righteous demands of the divine law. This is said to be "toward God," because seeing Him to be the party dishonored by sin, it feels all its acknowledgments and compunctions to be properly due to Him, as the great Lawgiver, and directs them to Him accordingly; condemning, humbling itself, and grieving before Him, looking also to Him as its only Hope of deliverance. Faith is said to be "toward our Lord Jesus Christ," because in that frame of mind just described it eagerly credits the testimony of relief divinely provided in Christ, gladly embraces the overtures of reconciliation in Him, and directs all its expectations of salvation, from its first stage to its last, to Him as the one appointed Medium of all grace from God to a sinful world. Thus we have here a brief summary of all Gospel preaching. And it is easy to see why repentance is here put before faith; for the former must of necessity precede the latter. There is a repentance subsequent to faith, the fruit of felt pardon and restoration. It was this which drew the tears with which the Saviour's feet were once so copiously moistened. (<reference osisRef="Luke.7.37">Lu 7:37</reference>, 38, 47; and compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.63">Eze 16:63</reference>). But that is not the light in which it is here presented. <div eID="gen31154" type="x-p"/>
entries.c23442677e802e061281d4b1a2dfebe1a36572e9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16112"/><div sID="gen31155" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16112"/><hi type="bold">22-23. And now, behold, I--</hi>"I" is emphatic here.<div eID="gen31155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31156" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bound in the spirit--</hi>compare <reference osisRef="Acts.19.21">Ac 19:21</reference>. This internal pressure, unattended with any knowledge of "what was to befall him there," was the result of that higher guidance which shaped all his movements. <div eID="gen31156" type="x-p"/>
entries.dd174259857d8cdd561f10e2f76627f0d0340cd0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16114"/><div sID="gen31158" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16114"/><hi type="bold">24. But none of these things move me, neither, &c.--</hi>In this noble expression of absolute dedication to the service of Christ and preparedness for the worst that could befall him in such a cause, note (1) his jealousy for the peculiar character of his mission, as immediately from Christ Himself on which all the charges against him turned; (2) the burden of that Gospel which he preached--Grace; it was "the Gospel of the Grace of God." <div eID="gen31158" type="x-p"/>
entries.750f3a4b8d04db50ff9fee0a6fbe638ea39d013b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16115"/><div sID="gen31159" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16115"/><hi type="bold">25-27. I know that ye all ... shall see my face no more--</hi>not an inspired prediction of what was certainly to be, but what the apostle, in his peculiar circumstances, fully expected. Whether, therefore, he ever did see them again, is a question to be decided purely on its own evidence. <div eID="gen31159" type="x-p"/>
entries.e03fef95a6a6a17ef537a212eea5579fd3db38cb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16118"/><div sID="gen31162" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16118"/><hi type="bold">28. Take heed ... unto yourselves--</hi>Compare 1Ti 3:2-7; 4:16; 6:11.<div eID="gen31162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31163" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and to all the flock--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="Heb.13.17">He 13:17</reference>. Observe here how the personal is put before the pastoral care.<div eID="gen31163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31164" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">over ... which the Holy Ghost hath made you--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="John.20.22">Joh 20:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.20.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.8">Ep 4:8</reference>, 11, 12; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.1">Re 3:1</reference>. (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.23">Ac 14:23</reference> shows that the apostle did not mean to exclude human ordination).<div eID="gen31164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31165" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">overseers--</hi>or, as the same word is everywhere else rendered in our version, "bishops." The English Version has hardly dealt fair in this case with the sacred text, in rendering the word "overseers," whereas it ought here, as in all other places, to have been "bishops," in order that the fact of elders and bishops having been originally and apostolically synonymous, might be apparent to the ordinary English reader, which now it is not [Alford]. The distinction between these offices cannot be certainly traced till the second century, nor was it established till late in that century.<div eID="gen31165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31166" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to feed the church of God--</hi>or, "the Church of the Lord." Which of these two readings of the text is the true one, is a question which has divided the best critics. The evidence of manuscripts preponderates in favor of "THE Lord"; some of the most ancient Versions, though not all, so read; and Athanasius, the great champion of the supreme Divinity of Christ early in the fourth century, says the expression "Church of God" is unknown to the Scriptures. Which reading, then, does the internal evidence favor? As "Church of God" occurs nine times elsewhere in Paul's writings, and "Church of the Lord" nowhere, the probability, it is said, is that he used his wonted phraseology here also. But if he did, it is extremely difficult to see how so many early transcribers should have altered it into the quite unusual phrase, "Church of the Lord"; whereas, if the apostle did use this latter expression, and the historian wrote it so accordingly, it it easy to see how transcribers might, from being so accustomed to the usual phrase, write it "Church of God." On the whole, therefore, we accept the second reading as most probably the true one. But see what follows.<div eID="gen31166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31167" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which he hath purchased--</hi>"made His own," "acquired."<div eID="gen31167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31168" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with his own blood--</hi>"His own" is emphatic: "That glorified Lord who from the right hand of power in the heavens is gathering and ruling the Church, and by His Spirit, through human agency, hath set you over it, cannot be indifferent to its welfare in your hands, seeing He hath given for it His own most precious blood, thus making it His own by the dearest of all ties." The transcendent sacredness of the Church of Christ is thus made to rest on the dignity of its Lord and the consequent preciousness of that blood which He shed for it. And as the sacrificial atoning character of Christ's death is here plainly expressed, so His supreme dignity is implied as clearly by the second reading as it is expressed by the first. What a motive to pastoral fidelity is here furnished! <div eID="gen31168" type="x-p"/>
entries.5d2feb76376dc28379bdd13b665d20ca0f39e565: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16119"/><div sID="gen31169" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16119"/><hi type="bold">29-30. after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you--</hi>Two classes of coming enemies are here announced, the one more external to themselves, the other bred in the bosom of their own community; both were to be teachers, but the one, "grievous wolves," not sparing, that is, making a prey of the flock; the other (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.30">Ac 20:30</reference>), simply sectarian "perverters" of the truth, with the view of drawing a party after them. Perhaps the one pointed to that subtle poison of Oriental Gnosticism which we know to have very early infected the Asiatic churches; the other to such Judaizing tendencies as we know to have troubled nearly all the early churches. See the Epistles to the Ephesians, Colossians, and Timothy, also those to the seven churches of Asia (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.1-Rev.3.22">Re 2:1-3:22</reference>). But watchfulness against all that tends to injure and corrupt the Church is the duty of its pastors in every age. <div eID="gen31169" type="x-p"/>
entries.0ab20c5d6ff60ef55e1d6ad67d7ac9a2d9d36b84: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16120"/><div sID="gen31170" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16120"/><hi type="bold">31. by the space of three years--</hi>speaking in round numbers; for it was nearer three than two years.<div eID="gen31170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31171" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears--</hi>What an appeal to be able to make! "And if this was an apostle's part, how much more a pastor's!" [Bengel]. <div eID="gen31171" type="x-p"/>
entries.7bd2182b3eaa7301455afd959ad572966770563d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16121"/><div sID="gen31172" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16121"/><hi type="bold">32-35. I commend you to God--</hi>the almighty Conservator of His people.<div eID="gen31172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31173" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and to the word of his grace--</hi>that message of His pure grace (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.24">Ac 20:24</reference>) by the faith of which He keeps us (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.5">1Pe 1:5</reference>).<div eID="gen31173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31174" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which--</hi>that is, God.<div eID="gen31174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31175" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is able to build you up, and to give you an inheritance, &c.--</hi>Observe how salvation--not only in its initial stages of pardon and regeneration, but in all its subsequent stages of "up-building," even to its consummation in the final inheritance--is here ascribed to the "ability" of God to bestow it, as in <reference osisRef="Rom.16.25">Ro 16:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.20">Ep 3:20</reference>; particularly Jude 24; and compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.12">2Ti 1:12</reference>, where the same thing is ascribed to Christ.<div eID="gen31175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31176" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">among all them which are sanctified--</hi>Sanctification is here viewed as the final character and condition of the heirs of glory, regarded as one saved company. <div eID="gen31176" type="x-p"/>
entries.35e862445083e7ffa9bdad649b91f90b7c9694d8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16124"/><div sID="gen31182" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16124"/><hi type="bold">36-38. he kneeled down and prayed with them all, &c.--</hi>Nothing can be more touching than these three concluding verses, leaving an indelible impression of rare ministerial fidelity and affection on the apostle's part, and of warm admiration and attachment on the part of these Ephesian presbyters. Would to God that such scenes were more frequent in the Church! <chapter eID="Acts.20"/>

entries.775177a0b7a8b8b6223b3158b4c5c08ca2c7f79c: <div eID="gen45082" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen45083" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen45084" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen45084" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen45083" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen45085" type="x-p"/> Paul retires to Macedonia, <reference osisRef="Act.20.1">Act 20:1</reference>. He goes into Greece, where he tarries three months and, purposing to sail to Syria, he returns through Macedonia, <reference osisRef="Act.20.2">Act 20:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.20.3">Act 20:3</reference>. Several persons accompany him into Asia, and then go before and tarry for him at Troas, <reference osisRef="Act.20.4">Act 20:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.20.5">Act 20:5</reference>. Paul and Luke sail from Philippi, and in five days reach Troas, where they meet their brethren from Asia, and abide there seven days, <reference osisRef="Act.20.6">Act 20:6</reference>. On the first day of the week, the disciples coming together to break bread, Paul preaching to them, and continuing his speech till midnight, a young man of the name of Eutychus, being in a deep sleep, fell from the third loft and was killed, <reference osisRef="Act.20.7-Act.20.9">Act 20:7-9</reference>. Paul restores him to life, resumes his discourse, and continuing it till daybreak, then departs, <reference osisRef="Act.20.10-Act.20.12">Act 20:10-12</reference>. Luke and his companions come to Assos, whither Paul comes by land, <reference osisRef="Act.20.13">Act 20:13</reference>. He embarks with them at Assos, comes to Mitylene, <reference osisRef="Act.20.14">Act 20:14</reference>. Sails thence, and passes by Chios, arrives at Samos, tarries at Trogyllium, and comes to Miletus, <reference osisRef="Act.20.15">Act 20:15</reference>. Purposing to get as soon as possible to Jerusalem, he sends from Miletus, and calls the elders of the Church of Ephesus, to whom he preaches a most directing sermon, gives them the most solemn exhortations, kneels down and prays with them, takes a very affecting leave of them, and sets sail for Caesarea, in order to go to Jerusalem, vv. 16-38. <div eID="gen45085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45086" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen45086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45087" type="x-p"/> After the uproar was ceased - The tumult excited by Demetrius apparently induced Paul to leave Ephesus sooner than he had intended. He had written to the Corinthians that he should leave that place after pentecost, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.8">1Cor 16:8</reference>; but it is very probable that he left it sooner.
entries.50a740519efed60e6964d986ad39de63807fc55d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen45087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45088" type="x-p"/> He came into Greece - Εις την Ἑλλαδα, Into Hellas, Greece properly so called, the regions between Thessaly and Propontis, and the country of Achaia. He did not, however, go there immediately: he passed through Macedonia, <reference osisRef="Act.20.1">Act 20:1</reference>, in which he informs us, <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.5-2Cor.7.7">2Cor 7:5-7</reference>, that he suffered much, both from believers and infidels; but was greatly comforted by the arrival of Titus, who gave him a very flattering account of the prosperous state of the Church at Corinth. A short time after this, being still in Macedonia, he sent Titus back to Corinth, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.16">2Cor 8:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.17">2Cor 8:17</reference>, and sent by him the second epistle which he wrote to that Church, as Theodoret and others suppose. Some time after, he visited Corinth himself, according to his promise, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.5">1Cor 16:5</reference>. This was his third voyage to that city, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.14">2Cor 12:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.1">2Cor 13:1</reference>. What he did there at this time cannot be distinctly known; but, according to St. Augustin, he ordered every thing relative to the holy eucharist, and the proper manner in which it was to be received. See Calmet.
entries.c04ef21a7cb8bfc5d694bf38449a87e548876b74: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen45088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45089" type="x-p"/> Abode three months - Partly, as we may suppose, at Corinth, at Athens, and in Achaia; from which place he is supposed to have sent his epistle to the Romans, because he continued longer here than at any other place, and mentions several of the Corinthians in his salutations to the believers of Rome. <div eID="gen45089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45090" type="x-p"/> When the Jesus laid wait for him - Paul had determined to go by sea to Syria, and from thence to Jerusalem. This was the first object of his journey; and this was the readiest road he could take; but, hearing that the Jews had laid wait for him, probably to attack his ship on the voyage, seize his person, sell him for a slave, and take the money which he was carrying to the poor saints at Jerusalem, he resolved to go as much of the journey as he conveniently could, by land. Therefore, he returned through Macedonia, and from thence to Troas, where he embarked to sail for Syria, on his way to Jerusalem. The whole of his journey is detailed in this and the following chapter. See also the map.
entries.332910dd06aa7c68870486d2a71fac68d2800c3b: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen45090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45091" type="x-p"/> And there accompanied him - Rather, says Bishop Pearce, there followed him as far as to Asia; for they were not in his company till he set sail from Philippi, and came to them at Troas, in Asia, whither they had gone before, and where they tarried for him, <reference osisRef="Act.20.5">Act 20:5</reference>. <div eID="gen45091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45092" type="x-p"/> Into Asia - Αχρι της Ασιας; These words are wanting in two MSS., Erpen, the Ethiopic, Coptic, and Vulgate. Some think that they embarrass this place; for how these could accompany him into Asia, and go before him, and tarry for him at Troas, <reference osisRef="Act.20.6">Act 20:6</reference>, is not so very clear; unless we suppose, what I have glanced at in the table of contents, that they came with him to Asia, but, he tarrying a short time, they proceeded on their journey, and stopped for him at Troas, where he shortly after rejoined them. Mr. Wakefield gets rid of the difficulty by reading the verse thus: Now Sopater of Berea accompanied him; but Aristarchus and Secundus of Thessalonica, Gaius of Derbe, Timothy of Lystra, and Tychicus and Trophimus of Asia, went before, and tarried for us at Troas. <div eID="gen45092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45093" type="x-p"/> Sopater of Berea - Sopater seems to be the same as Sosipater, whom St. Paul mentions as his kinsman, <reference osisRef="Rom.16.21">Rom 16:21</reference>. ADE, more than twenty others, with the Coptic, Armenian, later Syriac in the margin, Vulgate, Itala, Theophylact, Origen, and Bede, add Πυρῥου, Sopater the Son of Pyrrhus. Griesbach has received this into his text. <div eID="gen45093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45094" type="x-p"/> Aristarchus of Thessalonica - This person occurs in <reference osisRef="Act.19.29">Act 19:29</reference>, and is mentioned there as a Macedonian. He attended Paul in his journey to Rome, <reference osisRef="Act.27.2">Act 27:2</reference>, and was his fellow laborer, <reference osisRef="Plm.1.24">Plm 1:24</reference>, and his fellow prisoner, <reference osisRef="Col.4.10">Col 4:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.4.11">Col 4:11</reference>. Secundus is mentioned nowhere but in this place. <div eID="gen45094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45095" type="x-p"/> Gaius of Derbe - This is supposed to be the same who is mentioned <reference osisRef="Act.19.26">Act 19:26</reference>, and who is there called a man of Macedonia, of which some suppose he was a native, but descended from a family that came from Derbe; but as Gaius, or Caius, was a very common name, these might have been two distinct persons. One of this name was baptized by St. Paul at Corinth, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.14">1Cor 1:14</reference>, and entertained him as his host while he abode there, <reference osisRef="Rom.16.23">Rom 16:23</reference>, and was probably the same to whom St. John directs his third epistle. <div eID="gen45095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45096" type="x-p"/> And Timotheus - Of Lystra, is added by the Syriac. This was the same person of whom mention is made, <reference osisRef="Act.16.1">Act 16:1</reference>, and to whom St. Paul wrote the two epistles which are still extant; and who was a native of Lystra, as we learn from the above place. It was on this evidence, probably that the ancient Syriac translator added, of Lystra, to the text. This reading is not supported by any MSS. <div eID="gen45096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45097" type="x-p"/> Tychicus - of Asia - This person was high in the confidence of St. Paul. He styles him a beloved brother, and faithful minister in the Lord, whom he sent to the Ephesians, that he might know their affairs, and comfort their hearts, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.21">Eph 6:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.22">Eph 6:22</reference>. He sent him for the same purpose, and with the same commendations, to the Colossians, <reference osisRef="Col.4.7">Col 4:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.4.8">Col 4:8</reference>. Paul seems also to have designed him to superintend the Church at Crete in the absence of Titus; see <reference osisRef="Tit.3.12">Tit 3:12</reference>. He seems to have been the most intimate and confidential friend that Paul had. <div eID="gen45097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45098" type="x-p"/> Trophimus - Was an Ephesian; and both he and Tychicus are called Εφεσιοι, Ephesians, instead of Ασιανοι, Asiatics, in the Codex Bezae, both Greek and Latin, and in the Sahidic. He accompanied Paul from Ephesus into Greece, as we see here; and from thence to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Act.21.29">Act 21:29</reference>. He had, no doubt, traveled with him on other journeys, for we find, by <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.20">2Tim 4:20</reference>, that he was obliged to leave him sick at Miletus, being then, as it is likely, on his return to his own kindred at Ephesus.
entries.8f646d527769d498ad5532bacc6cd5fdbb29d466: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen45098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45099" type="x-p"/> Tarried for us at Troas - See the preceding verse. Troas was a small town in Phrygia Minor, in the province called the Troad: see <reference osisRef="Act.16.8">Act 16:8</reference>.
entries.6dd13a4fb51d69a202a999613d9e6da12792e366: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen45099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45100" type="x-p"/> Days of unleavened bread - The seven days of the passover, in which they ate unleavened bread. See the account of this festival in the notes on Exodus 12:1-51 (note). It is evident, from the manner in which St. Luke writes here, that he had not been with St. Paul since the time he accompanied him to Philippi, <reference osisRef="Act.16.10-Act.16.12">Act 16:10-12</reference>; but he now embarks at Philippi with the apostle, and accompanies him to Troas, and continues with him through the rest of his journey. <div eID="gen45100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45101" type="x-p"/> To Troas in five days - So long they were making this voyage from Philippi, being obliged to keep always by the coast, and in sight of the land; for the magnetic needle was not yet known. See the situation of these places upon the map.
entries.085fd5dbe4f3f719cf93c1da5f00a5e2e9a0cd62: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen45101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45102" type="x-p"/> Upon the first day of the week - What was called κυριακη, the Lord's day, the Christian Sabbath, in which they commemorated the resurrection of our Lord; and which, among all Christians, afterwards took the place of the Jewish Sabbath. <div eID="gen45102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45103" type="x-p"/> To break bread - To break eucaristia, the eucharist, as the Syriac has it; intimating, by this, that they were accustomed to receive the holy sacrament on each Lord's day. It is likely that, besides this, they received a common meal together. Some think the αγαπη, or love feast, is intended. <div eID="gen45103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45104" type="x-p"/> Continued his speech until midnight - At what time he began to preach we cannot tell, but we hear when he concluded. He preached during the whole night, for he did not leave off till the break of the next day, <reference osisRef="Act.20.11">Act 20:11</reference>, though about midnight his discourse was interrupted by the fall of Eutychus. As this was about the time of pentecost, and we may suppose about the beginning of May, as Troas was in about 40 degrees of north latitude, the sun set there at seven p.m. and rose at five a.m., so that the night was about eight hours long; and taking all the interruptions together, and they could not have amounted to more than two hours, and taking no account of the preceding day's work, Paul must have preached a sermon not less than six hours long. But it is likely that a good part of this time was employed in hearing and answering questions; for διελεγετο, and διαλεγομενου, may be thus understood.
entries.3bf955c4488dd92ae2d97c0d77417dd15c403b93: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen45104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45105" type="x-p"/> Upper chamber - It was in an upper chamber in the temple that the primitive disciples were accustomed to meet: on that account, they might have preferred an upper chamber whenever they could meet with it. The pious Quesnel supposes that the smoke, issuing from the many lamps in this upper chamber, was the cause of Eutychus falling asleep; and this, he says, the apostle mentions, in charity, to excuse the young man's appearing negligent.
entries.a3063915325f649b1e3a51375d01d20bb938f0bc: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen45105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45106" type="x-p"/> There sat in a window - This was probably an opening in the wall, to let in light and air, for there was no glazing at that time; and it is likely that Eutychus fell backward through it, down to the ground, on the outside; there being nothing to prevent his falling out, when he had once lost the power to take care of himself, by getting into a deep sleep.
entries.a3c671978d19c5e7f7152632a37bf1580c0c66e8: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen45106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45107" type="x-p"/> And Paul - fell on him - Επεπεσεν αυτῳ, Stretched himself upon him, in the same manner as Elisha did on the Shunammite's son, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.33-2Kgs.4.35">2Kgs 4:33-35</reference>; though the action of lying on him, in order to communicate warmth to the flesh, might not have been continued so long as in the above instance; nor indeed was it necessary, as the natural warmth had not yet left the body of Eutychus; but the son of the Shunammite had been some time dead.
entries.ad0234f817ba152bca3a5d3cfc0b70275f28d5da: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen45107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45108" type="x-p"/> Had broken bread - Had taken some refreshment, in order to their journey. <div eID="gen45108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45109" type="x-p"/> And talked a long while - Ὁμιλησας, Having familiarly conversed, for this is the import of the word, which is very different from the διελεγετο, of the seventh verse, and the διαλεγομενου, of the ninth; which imply solemn, grave discourse.
entries.c627dca6b8d468f3f40ebbf7f0c9bb58d0d41522: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen45109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45110" type="x-p"/> Sailed unto Assos - Assos, according to Pausanias, Eliac. ii. 4, and Pliny, Hist. Nat. xxxvi. 27, was a maritime town of Asia, in the Troad. Strabo and Stephanus place it in Mysia. It was also called Apollonia, according to Pliny, Ib. lib. <reference osisRef="Act.20.30">Act 20:30</reference>. The passage by sea to this place was much longer than by land; and therefore St. Paul chose to go by land, while the others went by sea. <div eID="gen45110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45111" type="x-p"/> Intending to take in Paul - Αναλαμβανειν, To take him in Again; for it appears he had already been aboard that same vessel: probably the same that had carried them from Philippi to Troas, <reference osisRef="Act.20.6">Act 20:6</reference>.
entries.dd263aa2f7ea2913eaf626271b2bf95efd8718e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen45111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45112" type="x-p"/> Came to Mitylene - This was a seaport town in the isle of Lesbos: see its place in the map.
entries.bcc8ae7f4062c79495d6720ccdc32cadaad8cefa: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen45112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45113" type="x-p"/> Over against Chios - This was a very celebrated island between Lesbos and Samos, famous in antiquity for its extraordinary wines. At this island the apostle did not touch. <div eID="gen45113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45114" type="x-p"/> Arrived at Samos - This was another island of the Aegean Sea, or Archipelago. It does not appear that they landed at Samos: they passed close by it, and anchored at Trogyllium. This was a promontory of Ionia, which gave name to some small islands in the vicinity of Samos: Της δε Τρωγιλιου προκειται νησιον ὁμωνυμον: before Trogyllium is situated an island of the same name. Strabo, lib. xiv. p. 635. Pliny also mentions this place, Hist. Nat. lib. v. cap. 31. Near this place was the mouth of the famous river Maeander. <div eID="gen45114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45115" type="x-p"/> Came to Miletus - A celebrated city in the province of Caria, about twelve or fifteen leagues from Ephesus, according to Calmet. Miletus is famous for being the birthplace of Thales, one of the seven wise men of Greece, and founder of the Ionic sect of philosophers. Anaximander was also born here, and several other eminent men. The Turks, who lately possessed it, call it Melas.
entries.41b770e964fa4ea13cbd43d0874adecc2a723b90: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen45115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45116" type="x-p"/> To sail by Ephesus - Not to touch there at this time. <div eID="gen45116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45117" type="x-p"/> To be at Jerusalem the day of pentecost - That he might have the opportunity of preaching the kingdom of God to multitudes of Jews from different places, who would come up to Jerusalem at that feast; and then he no doubt expected to see there a renewal of that day of pentecost in which the Spirit was poured out on the disciples, and in consequence of which so many were converted to God.
entries.6e5134b7a7114d45650b781e54092436c6229dbf: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen45117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45118" type="x-p"/> He sent to Ephesus, and called the elders of the Church - These are called επισκοποι, bishops, <reference osisRef="Act.20.28">Act 20:28</reference>. By the πρεσβυτεροι, presbyters or elders, here, we are to understand all that were in authority in the Church, whether they were επισκοποι, bishops or overseers, or seniors in years, knowledge, and experience. The πρεσβυτεροι, or elders, were probably the first order in the Church; an order which was not so properly constituted, but which rose out of the state of things. From these presbuteroi the episcopoi, overseers or superintendents, were selected. Those who were eldest in years, Christian knowledge, and experience, would naturally be preferred to all others, as overseers of the Church of Christ. From the Greek word πρεσβυτερος, comes the Latin presbyterus, the English presbyter, the French prestre, and our own term priest; and all, when traced up to their original, signify merely an elderly or aged person; though it soon became the name of an office, rather than of a state of years. Now, as these elders are called επισκοποι, bishops, in <reference osisRef="Act.20.28">Act 20:28</reference>, we may take it for granted that they were the same order; or, rather, that these superintendents of the Church were indifferently called either presbyters or bishops. <div eID="gen45118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45119" type="x-p"/> As he had not time to call at Ephesus, he thought it best to have a general convocation of the heads of that Church, to meet him at Miletus, that he might give them the instructions mentioned in the succeeding parts of this chapter.
entries.cd833c37b2385db274e1968a4732c2cf5e130b79: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen45119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45120" type="x-p"/> After what manner I have been with you - The Codex Bezae adds here, for three years, and even more, which reading might have been borrowed from <reference osisRef="Act.20.31">Act 20:31</reference>, though the time assigned by it is too long.
entries.b2d05251f41611b9273119215b7e6c8368289260: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen45120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45121" type="x-p"/> Serving the Lord with all humility, etc. - This relates not only to his zealous and faithful performance of his apostolic functions, but also to his private walk as a Christian; and shows with what carefulness this apostle himself was obliged to walk, in order to have his calling and election, as a Christian, ratified and made firm.
entries.660d665e84163625bdedfd3027f5eb1710c721ad: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen45121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45122" type="x-p"/> I kept back nothing - Notwithstanding the dangers to which he was exposed, and the temptations he must have had to suppress those truths that were less acceptable to the unrenewed nature of man, or to the particular prejudices of the Jews and the Gentiles, he fully and faithfully, at all hazards, declared what he terms, <reference osisRef="Act.20.27">Act 20:27</reference>, the whole counsel of God. "Behold here," says the judicious and pious Calmet, "the model of a good shepherd - full of doctrine and zeal: he communicates with profusion, and yet with discretion, without jealousy and without fear, what God had put in his heart, and what charity inspires. A good shepherd, says St. Bernard, should always have abundance of bread in his scrip, and his dog under command. His dog is his zeal, which he must lead, order, and moderate; his scrip full of bread is his mind full of useful knowledge; and he should ever be in readiness to give nourishment to his flock." He who will quarrel with this sentiment, because of the uncouthness of the simile, needs pity, and deserves censure.
entries.82837fe2d78f0ddec1934e021bcb3f502d150a53: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen45122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45123" type="x-p"/> Testify both to - Jews and - Greeks - He always began with the Jews; and, in this case, he had preached to them alone for three months, <reference osisRef="Act.19.8-Act.19.10">Act 19:8-10</reference>, and only left their synagogues when he found, through their obstinacy, he could do them no good. <div eID="gen45123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45124" type="x-p"/> Repentance toward God, etc. - As all had sinned against God, so all should humble themselves before him against whom they have sinned; but humiliation is no atonement for sin; therefore repentance is insufficient, unless faith in our Lord Jesus Christ accompany it. Repentance disposes and prepares the soul for pardoning mercy; but can never be considered as making compensation for past acts of transgression. This repentance and faith were necessary to the salvation both of Jews and Gentiles; for all had sinned, and come short of God's glory. The Jews must repent, who had sinned so much, and so long, against light and knowledge. The Gentiles must repent, whose scandalous lives were a reproach to man. Faith in Jesus Christ was also indispensably necessary; for a Jew might repent, be sorry for his sin, and suppose that, by a proper discharge of his religious duty, and bringing proper sacrifices, he could conciliate the favor of God: No, this will not do; nothing but faith in Jesus Christ, as the end of the law, and the great and only vicarious sacrifice, will do; hence he testified to them the necessity of faith in this Messiah. The Gentiles might repent of their profligate lives, turn to the true God, and renounce all idolatry: this is well, but it is not sufficient: they also have sinned, and their present amendment and faith can make no atonement for what is past; therefore, they also must believe on the Lord Jesus, who died for their sins, and rose again for their justification.
entries.0f20a71f0cbae13f67c6df01451b8ef251d96785: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen45124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45125" type="x-p"/> I go bound in the spirit - Δεδεμενος τῳ πνευματι - Either meaning the strong influence of the Divine Spirit upon his mind, or the strong propensity in his own will, wish, and desire, to visit Jerusalem; and in this sense δεειν, to bind, is sometimes used. But it appears more consistent with the mind of the apostle, and with that influence under which we find that he constantly acted, to refer it to the influence of the Holy Ghost; ὑπο του πνευματος, being under the power of that Spirit; as if he had said: "I have now no choice - God has not left me either to the advices of friends, or to my own prudence: the Spirit of God obliges me to go to Jerusalem, and yet does not intimate to me what peculiar trials shall befall me there: I have only the general intimation that, in every city where I proclaim the Gospel, bonds and afflictions await me." This sense of the word Kypke has largely defended in his note here.
entries.3fce5176cad12640ef3c9405f6f44df71fe939cb: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen45125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45126" type="x-p"/> None of these things move me - Ουδενος λογον ποιουμαι; I consider them as nothing; I value them not a straw; they weigh not with me. <div eID="gen45126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45127" type="x-p"/> Neither count I my life dear - I am not my own; my life and being are the Lord's; he requires me to employ them in his service; I act under his direction, and am not anxious about the issue. <div eID="gen45127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45128" type="x-p"/> Finish my course with joy - Τον δρομον μου, My ministerial function. We have already met with this word in application to the same subject, <reference osisRef="Act.13.25">Act 13:25</reference>, where see the note. And the apostle here adds, by way of explanation, και την διακονιαν, even that ministry which I have received of the Lord. The words μετα χαρας, with joy, are omitted by ABD, some others; the Syriac, Erpen, Coptic, Sahidic, Ethiopic, Vulgate, and some of the fathers. If we consider them as genuine they may imply thus much: that the apostle wished to fulfill his ministry in such a way as might meet with the Divine approbation; for nothing could give him joy that did not please and glorify God. <div eID="gen45128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45129" type="x-p"/> To testify - Διαμαρτυρασθαι, Earnestly, solemnly, and strenuously to assert, vindicate, and prove the Gospel of the grace of God, not only to be in itself what it professes to be, but to be also the power of God for salvation to every one that believes.
entries.f8412b9b486bb0c6f952e992c402623bcb2ef300: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen45129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45130" type="x-p"/> Ye all - shall see my face no more - This probably refers simply to the persons who were now present; concerning whom he might have had a Divine intimation, that they should not be found in life when he should come that way again. Or it may refer only to Ephesus and Miletus. From the dangers to which he was exposed, it was, humanly speaking, unlikely that he should ever return; and this may be all that is implied: but that he did revisit those parts, though probably not Miletus or Ephesus, appears likely from <reference osisRef="Phi.1.25-Phi.1.27">Phi 1:25-27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phi.2.24">Phi 2:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Plm.1.22">Plm 1:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.19-Heb.13.23">Heb 13:19-23</reference>. But in all these places he speaks with a measure of uncertainty: he had not an absolute evidence that he should not return; but, in his own mind, it was a matter of uncertainty. The Holy Spirit did not think proper to give him a direct revelation on this point.
entries.d5bb6c205d88202299ac8c9022d5f2831b4de628: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen45130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45131" type="x-p"/> I am pure from the blood of all - If any man, Jew or Gentile, perish in his sins, his blood shall be upon him; he, alone, shall be accessary to his own perdition.
